questions.question: What provides the stabilising attraction in an ionic solid?
options: Attraction between oppositely charged ions throughout an extended lattice
Shared electron density confined between every pair of metal atoms
Rapid switching among separate resonance molecules
London dispersion forces between isolated ion pairs
questions.explanation: Ionic bonding is an electrostatic attraction distributed through an extended crystal lattice. Treating the solid as isolated ion pairs misses the many-ion nature of its stability.
questions.sourceEvidence: Ionic bonding is the attraction between oppositely charged ions in an extended lattice, commonly formed after substantial electron transfer.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating an ionic crystal as independent molecule-like ion pairs.

questions.question: How are electrons distributed in a covalent bond?
options: They are completely transferred to form an extended ionic lattice
Their density is shared between the bonded nuclei
They are delocalised equally across every atom in a metal
They occupy no region between the nuclei
questions.explanation: A covalent bond involves electron density shared between nuclei. Complete transfer describes an idealised ionic limit rather than covalent bonding.
questions.sourceEvidence: Covalent bonding involves shared electron density between nuclei, while metallic bonding involves delocalised valence electrons distributed across many atomic centres.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing covalent electron sharing with complete electron transfer.

questions.question: Which electron arrangement best describes metallic bonding?
options: Localised lone pairs fixed on every atomic centre
Alternating complete transfers between neighboring atoms
Delocalised valence electrons spread across many atomic centres
One shared electron pair restricted to each pair of nuclei
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding distributes valence electrons across many atomic centres. Restricting each electron pair to two nuclei instead describes a localised covalent picture.
questions.sourceEvidence: Covalent bonding involves shared electron density between nuclei, while metallic bonding involves delocalised valence electrons distributed across many atomic centres.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Modeling metallic bonding as a collection of localised two-atom covalent bonds.

questions.question: Why is an electronegativity difference not a universal bond-type cutoff?
options: Electronegativity applies only to metallic elements
Every bond has exactly equal ionic and covalent character
Only formal charge can indicate electron distribution
Bonding forms a continuum, and local structure and element identity also matter
questions.explanation: Electronegativity difference is a useful estimate rather than a rigid boundary. Real bonding character also depends on structure and the elements involved.
questions.sourceEvidence: Bonding is a continuum rather than three perfectly separated categories. Electronegativity difference helps estimate bond polarity, but local structure and the elements involved also matter.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assigning bond type from a rigid electronegativity threshold alone.

questions.question: What distinguishes a polar covalent bond from an equal-sharing covalent bond?
options: Its unequal electron sharing produces partial charges
Its electrons are absent from the internuclear region
It must occur only between a metal and a nonmetal
It consists of isolated full ions in a repeating lattice
questions.explanation: A polar covalent bond shares electron density unequally and develops partial charges. Partial charges do not mean that the bonded atoms have become isolated full ions.
questions.sourceEvidence: A polar covalent bond has unequal electron sharing and partial charges; an ionic solid is not a collection of isolated molecule pairs but a repeating crystal whose stability reflects attractions and repulsions across the entire lattice.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Equating partial charges in a polar covalent bond with full ionic charges.

questions.question: Which information can a Lewis structure track directly?
options: Exact three-dimensional bond angles and orbital energies
Valence electrons, bonding pairs, lone pairs, and formal charge
Measured partial charges and magnetic behaviour
The complete excited-state molecular-orbital spectrum
questions.explanation: Lewis structures are electron-bookkeeping models for valence electrons, pairs, and formal charge. They do not directly provide a complete three-dimensional or orbital-energy description.
questions.sourceEvidence: Lewis structures track valence electrons, bonding pairs, lone pairs, and formal charge. They are useful bookkeeping models but do not directly show three-dimensional shape, orbital energies, or electron delocalisation.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming a Lewis structure directly displays exact shape and orbital energies.

questions.question: What do multiple resonance structures represent?
options: Separate molecules that rapidly interconvert at equilibrium
Different crystal phases with distinct atom positions
Alternative drawings of one delocalised electronic state
Proof that the molecule has no valid electron distribution
questions.explanation: Resonance drawings contribute to one delocalised electronic state. They are not snapshots of separate molecules switching back and forth.
questions.sourceEvidence: Resonance structures are alternative drawings of one delocalised electronic state, not molecules rapidly switching between forms.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Interpreting resonance contributors as distinct, rapidly interconverting molecules.

questions.question: How does increasing bond order generally affect a bond?
options: It makes the bond weaker and longer
It changes formal charge but never bond length
It eliminates electron density between the nuclei
It makes the bond stronger and shorter
questions.explanation: Greater bond order generally corresponds to increased bond strength and reduced bond length. The trend reflects more bonding interaction between the nuclei.
questions.sourceEvidence: Bond order generally correlates with greater bond strength and shorter bond length.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Believing that greater bond order produces a longer or weaker bond.

questions.question: What principle does VSEPR use to predict molecular shape?
options: Electron domains arrange around the central atom to minimise repulsion
Bonding electrons collapse into one side of the central atom
Only lone pairs determine the three-dimensional arrangement
Atomic mass fixes every molecular bond angle
questions.explanation: VSEPR spreads electron domains around a central atom to reduce their mutual repulsion. Both bonding domains and lone pairs participate in that arrangement.
questions.sourceEvidence: Valence-shell electron-pair repulsion theory predicts molecular shape by arranging electron domains around a central atom to minimise repulsion.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Ignoring bonding domains when applying electron-pair repulsion.

questions.question: When counting VSEPR electron domains, how is a triple bond treated?
options: As three bonding domains
As one bonding domain
As two bonding domains and one lone pair
As no domain because its electrons are shared
questions.explanation: A single, double, or triple bond each occupies one directional bonding domain. Counting individual bond components would overcount the domain geometry.
questions.sourceEvidence: Each single, double, or triple bond counts as one bonding domain, and each lone pair counts as one domain.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Counting a multiple bond as multiple VSEPR electron domains.

questions.question: Which electron-domain geometry corresponds to five domains around a central atom?
options: Tetrahedral
Octahedral
Trigonal bipyramidal
Trigonal planar
questions.explanation: Five electron domains adopt a trigonal-bipyramidal arrangement. Tetrahedral and octahedral geometries correspond to four and six domains, respectively.
questions.sourceEvidence: Two, three, four, five, and six domains adopt linear, trigonal-planar, tetrahedral, trigonal-bipyramidal, and octahedral electron-domain geometries.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Matching five electron domains to tetrahedral or octahedral geometry.

questions.question: Why can electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry have different names?
options: Molecular geometry counts multiple bonds as separate domains
Electron-domain geometry ignores bonding pairs
Electron-domain geometry applies only to diatomic molecules
Molecular geometry names atom positions and omits lone pairs
questions.explanation: Electron-domain geometry includes every bond and lone pair around the central atom. Molecular geometry describes only the positions of atoms, so hidden lone pairs can change its name.
questions.sourceEvidence: Molecular geometry names atomic positions and omits lone pairs from the shape name.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Using electron-domain and molecular-geometry labels interchangeably when lone pairs are present.

questions.question: CH4, NH3, and H2O each have four central electron domains. Why do their molecular shapes differ?
options: They have different numbers of central lone pairs
A multiple bond is counted as three domains in NH3
Hydrogen changes from positive to negative charge across the series
Their electron-domain geometries are linear, planar, and octahedral
questions.explanation: The three molecules share tetrahedral electron geometry but contain zero, one, and two central lone pairs. Omitting lone pairs from the molecular-shape name gives tetrahedral, trigonal-pyramidal, and bent shapes.
questions.sourceEvidence: Four domains give tetrahedral electron geometry, but CH4 is tetrahedral, NH3 is trigonal pyramidal, and H2O is bent because they contain zero, one, and two central lone pairs.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming equal electron-domain counts guarantee identical molecular shapes.

questions.question: Why are bond angles next to a lone pair often smaller than ideal?
options: Lone pairs have no electron density and pull atoms inward
Lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs
Every lone pair creates an additional visible atom
Bonding pairs always repel more strongly than lone pairs
questions.explanation: Lone pairs occupy more angular space and repel neighboring bonding domains strongly. That extra repulsion compresses the angles between visible bonds.
questions.sourceEvidence: Lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, so they compress adjacent bond angles below ideal values.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming lone pairs have less spatial influence than bonding pairs.

questions.question: Where does a lone pair preferentially sit in a trigonal-bipyramidal arrangement?
options: At an axial position with three 90-degree interactions
At the central atom with no directional domain
At an equatorial position with fewer 90-degree interactions
Between two axial positions as an extra seventh domain
questions.explanation: An equatorial site exposes a lone pair to fewer 90-degree interactions than an axial site. It therefore reduces repulsion more effectively.
questions.sourceEvidence: In trigonal-bipyramidal geometry, lone pairs prefer equatorial positions because these have fewer 90-degree interactions.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Placing a trigonal-bipyramidal lone pair axially despite an available equatorial site.

questions.question: For which class of structures should a VSEPR prediction be treated with particular caution?
options: Many simple main-group molecules
Any molecule containing a single bond
Every molecule with exactly four electron domains
Transition-metal complexes dominated by ligand and orbital effects
questions.explanation: VSEPR works well for many main-group molecules but is less reliable for transition-metal complexes. Detailed ligand interactions and orbital energetics can dominate those structures.
questions.sourceEvidence: VSEPR is highly effective for many main-group molecules but less reliable for transition-metal complexes or cases where ligand interactions and detailed orbital energetics dominate.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Applying main-group VSEPR rules uncritically to transition-metal complexes.

questions.question: How does valence-bond theory describe a covalent bond?
options: As overlap of half-filled atomic orbitals containing opposite-spin electrons
As complete removal of all valence orbitals from both atoms
As a lattice of full ions with no shared electron density
As a measured oscillation between separate resonance molecules
questions.explanation: Valence-bond theory forms a covalent bond through overlap of half-filled orbitals. The paired electrons in the overlap have opposite spins.
questions.sourceEvidence: Valence-bond theory describes a covalent bond as overlap between half-filled atomic orbitals containing opposite-spin electrons.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing orbital overlap in valence-bond theory with complete electron transfer.

questions.question: What is hybridisation in the orbital model?
options: A literal reaction an isolated atom completes before approaching another atom
A mathematical recombination that creates directional orbitals suited to bonding
The conversion of every sigma bond into a pi bond
A measurement of partial charge from electronegativity alone
questions.explanation: Hybridisation is a mathematical change of orbital basis used to describe directional bonding. It is not a directly observed preparatory rearrangement by an isolated atom.
questions.sourceEvidence: Hybridisation is a mathematical recombination of orbitals on one atom to produce directional hybrids suited to observed bonding.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating hybridisation as a literal pre-bonding event performed by an isolated atom.

questions.question: What results from mixing one s orbital with one p orbital?
options: One sp³ hybrid
Three sp² hybrids
Two sp hybrids
Two unhybridised s orbitals
questions.explanation: One s orbital and one p orbital recombine into two equivalent sp hybrids. The number of output orbitals equals the number mixed.
questions.sourceEvidence: Mixing one s and one p orbital produces two sp hybrids; adding two or three p orbitals produces three sp² or four sp³ hybrids.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing the number and type of hybrids produced by s-p orbital mixing.

questions.question: Which hybridisation-to-geometry pairing is correct?
options: sp is tetrahedral, sp² is linear, and sp³ is trigonal planar
sp is octahedral, sp² is tetrahedral, and sp³ is linear
All three hybridisations produce the same geometry
sp is linear, sp² is trigonal planar, and sp³ is tetrahedral
questions.explanation: Hybridisation correlates with local electron-domain geometry. The sp, sp², and sp³ models correspond to linear, trigonal-planar, and tetrahedral arrangements.
questions.sourceEvidence: Hybridisation correlates with electron-domain geometry: sp is linear, sp² is trigonal planar, and sp³ is tetrahedral.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Mismatching sp, sp², and sp³ hybridisation with their domain geometries.

questions.question: How does each carbon in ethene form its carbon-carbon double bond?
options: It uses sp² hybrids for sigma bonding and one unhybridised p orbital for the pi bond
It uses sp³ hybrids for two perpendicular pi bonds
It uses only unhybridised s orbitals for both bond components
It transfers one electron completely to the other carbon
questions.explanation: Each ethene carbon uses sp² hybrids for its sigma framework and retains one p orbital. Sideways overlap of those p orbitals forms the pi component.
questions.sourceEvidence: In ethene, each carbon uses sp² hybrids for three sigma bonds and retains one unhybridised p orbital; sideways p overlap forms the pi bond.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assigning an ethene carbon sp³ hybridisation or omitting its unhybridised p orbital.

questions.question: Why does each carbon in ethyne retain two unhybridised p orbitals?
options: Its sp³ hybridisation leaves all three p orbitals unused
Its sp hybridisation uses only one s and one p orbital
Its carbon-carbon bond contains no sigma component
Its two p orbitals are converted into lone pairs
questions.explanation: The sp model mixes one s and one p orbital, leaving two p orbitals unhybridised. Their perpendicular sideways overlaps form the two pi bonds of the triple bond.
questions.sourceEvidence: In ethyne, sp hybridisation leaves two unhybridised p orbitals on each carbon, producing two mutually perpendicular pi bonds around the carbon-carbon sigma bond.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming a carbon-carbon triple bond contains three sigma bonds or uses sp³ carbon.

questions.question: Why does a pi bond restrict rotation more than a sigma bond?
options: Its density is spherical and independent of orbital alignment
It contains no electrons between the bonded atoms
Its density lies above and below the internuclear axis and requires aligned sideways overlap
It is always weaker because it is an ionic interaction
questions.explanation: Pi bonding depends on side-by-side p-orbital alignment above and below the bond axis. Rotation would disrupt that overlap, whereas axial sigma overlap generally permits rotation.
questions.sourceEvidence: Sigma bonds have electron density concentrated along the internuclear axis and generally permit rotation, while pi bonds have density above and below that axis and restrict rotation.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming sigma and pi bonds permit rotation equally.

questions.question: When is molecular-orbital theory often more complete than a local hybridisation model?
options: Only when counting VSEPR lone pairs in water
Whenever a molecule contains one sigma bond
Only for assigning formal charge in a Lewis structure
When describing delocalisation, magnetism, and excited states
questions.explanation: Molecular-orbital theory can treat electron delocalisation, magnetism, and excited states more fully. Hybridisation remains useful for describing local bonding geometry.
questions.sourceEvidence: Molecular-orbital theory often provides a more complete description of delocalisation, magnetism, and excited states, but hybridisation remains a powerful local geometry model.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating hybridisation as a complete replacement for molecular-orbital descriptions.

questions.question: What produces a bond dipole?
options: Unequal attraction for shared electron density
Equal attraction for shared electron density
The absence of any electron density between nuclei
A compulsory transfer of a whole electron
questions.explanation: A bond dipole appears when bonded atoms attract the shared electrons unequally. This separation produces partial rather than necessarily full charges.
questions.sourceEvidence: A bond dipole results when bonded atoms attract shared electron density unequally.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming a bond dipole requires complete electron transfer.

questions.question: In the chemistry convention, where does the bond-dipole arrow point?
options: Toward the less electronegative atom
Toward the more electronegative atom
Always toward the atom with greater mass
Perpendicular to the bond regardless of atom identity
questions.explanation: The arrow points toward the atom that attracts shared density more strongly. A crossed tail marks the positive end.
questions.sourceEvidence: Chemistry convention draws a dipole arrow toward the more electronegative atom, often with a crossed tail at the positive end.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reversing the conventional bond-dipole arrow direction.

questions.question: How is a molecule’s overall polarity determined?
options: By selecting only its strongest bond dipole
By counting atoms without considering their positions
By adding all bond dipoles and lone-pair contributions as vectors
By assigning every covalent bond a full ionic charge
questions.explanation: Molecular polarity is a vector sum, so both magnitude and direction matter. Lone-pair contributions and three-dimensional geometry must be included.
questions.sourceEvidence: Molecular polarity is the vector sum of all bond dipoles and lone-pair contributions.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Predicting molecular polarity from one bond without vector addition.

questions.question: Why can CO2 and CCl4 have zero net dipole despite containing polar bonds?
options: Every bond in each molecule is nonpolar
Their lone pairs convert all bonds into metallic bonds
Their atoms exchange full electrons until all dipoles disappear
Their symmetric geometries make the bond-dipole vectors cancel
questions.explanation: Symmetry arranges equal bond-dipole vectors so their sum is zero. Polar bonds therefore do not automatically make the entire molecule polar.
questions.sourceEvidence: A molecule can contain polar bonds yet have zero net dipole if symmetry cancels them, as in linear CO2 or tetrahedral CCl4.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming any polar bond guarantees a polar molecule.

questions.question: Why do H2O and NH3 retain nonzero molecular dipoles?
options: Their bent and trigonal-pyramidal geometries prevent bond vectors from cancelling
Their bonds are perfectly symmetric and cancel
They contain only nonpolar bonds
They are extended ionic lattices rather than molecules
questions.explanation: The asymmetric bent and trigonal-pyramidal shapes leave an uncompensated vector sum. Their individual bond dipoles therefore combine into a net molecular dipole.
questions.sourceEvidence: Bent H2O and trigonal-pyramidal NH3 retain nonzero dipoles because their bond vectors do not cancel.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Ignoring molecular shape when adding the bond dipoles of H2O or NH3.

questions.question: What must be established before predicting whether bond dipoles cancel?
options: Only the total number of electrons
The molecule’s three-dimensional geometry
The boiling point of the pure substance
Whether the name contains a metal symbol
questions.explanation: Dipoles are vectors whose directions depend on the molecule’s geometry. A two-dimensional formula alone cannot establish whether those vectors cancel.
questions.sourceEvidence: Geometry must therefore be determined before polarity is predicted.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Predicting net polarity before determining molecular geometry.

questions.question: Which structural feature can enable especially strong hydrogen bonding?
options: Any carbon-carbon single bond
A perfectly symmetric nonpolar geometry alone
A suitable O–H, N–H, or F–H group
Only a metal-metal bond with delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: Suitable bonds to oxygen, nitrogen, or fluorine can support especially strong hydrogen bonds. Ordinary dipole-dipole attraction does not automatically have this specific strength and geometry.
questions.sourceEvidence: Polar molecules can exhibit dipole-dipole attractions; molecules containing suitable O–H, N–H, or F–H groups can form especially strong hydrogen bonds.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming every polar molecule forms hydrogen bonds equally strongly.

questions.question: Why do nonpolar substances still attract one another?
options: They all contain permanent full ionic charges
Their bond dipoles always add to a large permanent vector
They form covalent bonds between separate molecules during boiling
Instantaneous electron fluctuations create London dispersion forces
questions.explanation: Instantaneous fluctuations produce temporary attractions even in nonpolar substances. These London dispersion forces grow with polarisability and contact surface area.
questions.sourceEvidence: Nonpolar substances still experience London dispersion forces from instantaneous electron fluctuations, whose strength grows with polarisability and contact surface area.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Believing that nonpolar molecules have no intermolecular attractions.

questions.question: Why is a rigid electronegativity cutoff unreliable for assigning bond type?
options: Real bonding character forms a continuum rather than an absolute boundary
Electronegativity is unrelated to electron distribution
Every metal-nonmetal bond is fully covalent
Bond type depends only on molecular mass
questions.explanation: Bonding can mix ionic and covalent character, so one numerical cutoff is not universal. The local structure and elements must also be considered.
questions.sourceEvidence: Do not decide bond type from a rigid electronegativity cutoff or call every metal–nonmetal bond completely ionic.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Classifying every metal-nonmetal bond as completely ionic from a fixed cutoff.

questions.question: Why should formal charge not be reported as a measured partial charge?
options: Formal charge directly measures electron density in every molecule
Formal charge is a Lewis-structure bookkeeping assignment
Partial charge can exist only in ionic crystals
The two quantities are always numerically identical
questions.explanation: Formal charge follows an electron-bookkeeping convention for a Lewis structure. Measured partial charge describes an unequal distribution of actual electron density.
questions.sourceEvidence: Use formal charge for Lewis-structure bookkeeping, but remember that formal charge is not the same as measured partial charge.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Equating formal-charge bookkeeping with measured partial charge.

questions.question: Which interpretation of resonance forms is correct?
options: They are separate molecules rapidly reaching equilibrium
They show atoms changing positions between drawings
They are contributors to one delocalised electron distribution
They prove that no Lewis representation is useful
questions.explanation: Resonance contributors describe one delocalised electronic state. The molecule does not jump between independent structures.
questions.sourceEvidence: Resonance forms are not separate equilibrating molecules; the actual electron density is delocalised across the contributing structures.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating resonance contributors as separate equilibrating molecules.

questions.question: How should a multiple bond be counted in a VSEPR domain total?
options: As one domain for each bond line
As a lone pair plus one bond
It should be omitted from the count
As one electron domain
questions.explanation: VSEPR counts the direction occupied by a bond, not its individual sigma and pi components. A multiple bond therefore contributes one domain.
questions.sourceEvidence: For VSEPR, count electron domains around the central atom, treating any multiple bond as one domain.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Counting double or triple bonds as multiple VSEPR domains.

questions.question: Where should a trigonal-bipyramidal lone pair be placed when an equatorial site is available?
options: In an equatorial site to reduce 90-degree interactions
In an axial site to maximise 90-degree interactions
Outside the electron-domain count
At either site because all interactions are identical
questions.explanation: An equatorial lone pair has fewer 90-degree interactions and is energetically preferred. An axial placement creates unnecessary repulsion.
questions.sourceEvidence: Do not place trigonal-bipyramidal lone pairs axially when an equatorial location is available, and do not force VSEPR predictions onto transition-metal complexes without qualification.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Placing a trigonal-bipyramidal lone pair in an axial position by default.

questions.question: A molecule contains polar bonds. What additional step is needed before calling the molecule polar?
options: Count only the number of polar bonds
Add the bond dipoles as vectors using the three-dimensional geometry
Assume the largest dipole determines the whole molecule
Replace every partial charge with a full ionic charge
questions.explanation: Polar bonds may cancel when arranged symmetrically. The molecular geometry and vector sum determine whether a net dipole remains.
questions.sourceEvidence: A polar bond does not guarantee a polar molecule. Draw the three-dimensional geometry and add dipoles as vectors.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Inferring molecular polarity from the presence of a polar bond alone.

questions.question: When assigning hybridisation, how should pi bonds be treated?
options: Each pi bond is counted as an extra hybrid orbital
Every pi bond forces sp³ hybridisation
Pi bonds are ignored as extra domains when hybridisation follows local domain geometry
A pi bond replaces the sigma bond in a multiple bond
questions.explanation: Hybridisation follows the local electron-domain geometry and does not add a hybrid orbital for each pi bond. Unhybridised p orbitals form the pi components.
questions.sourceEvidence: Hybridisation follows local domain geometry and does not count pi bonds as extra hybrid orbitals.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Counting pi bonds as additional hybrid orbitals when assigning hybridisation.

questions.question: What usually happens to covalent molecules during boiling?
options: Their internal covalent bonds are all broken
Their nuclei and electrons separate completely
Every molecule becomes an extended ionic lattice
Intermolecular attractions are overcome while internal covalent bonds remain
questions.explanation: Boiling separates molecules by overcoming intermolecular attractions. It does not normally break the intramolecular covalent bonds that hold each molecule together.
questions.sourceEvidence: Always distinguish intramolecular bonds from intermolecular forces; boiling usually separates molecules without breaking their internal covalent bonds.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing intermolecular-force disruption during boiling with covalent-bond breaking.
